title: Notice to the Parties and the Profession — The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings (amended)
author: Federal Court of Canada

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The Federal Court’s notice supports conditional AI assistance while retaining court and litigant responsibility. It exemplifies the cluster’s certification/disclosure approach by requiring declarations for AI co-authorship, distinguishing advisory editing, and conditioning judicial use of automated decision-making on prior public consultation.
qs: A Declaration is required when the role AI plays in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation resembles that of a co-author.
For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The Federal Court guidance supports the cluster’s human-accountable governance model by requiring transparent disclosure of AI-generated filing content, urging reliance on reliable legal sources, and retaining institutional control over any future automated judicial decision-making through prior public consultation. Its disclosure mandate represents one jurisdiction-specific approach rather than a departure from the cluster’s broader convergence.
qs: This shall be done by a Declaration in the first paragraph stating that AI was used in preparing the document, either in its entirety or only for specifically identified paragraphs (the “Declaration”).
For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The Notice supports institution-wide supervision by requiring disclosure when AI directly generates litigation content, while exempting merely editorial assistance. It also preserves institutional control over court decision-making through prior public consultation and continuing stakeholder oversight. Its contribution is procedural and jurisdiction-specific rather than empirical.
qs: To ensure that the Court understands the role AI has played in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation, and submitted to the Court by or on behalf of a party or intervener, such materials must include the Declaration whenever they contain content created or generated directly by AI.
For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The Court supports the cluster’s core principle that humans remain accountable for AI-assisted filings and must verify AI-generated material under existing professional standards. It also exemplifies the cluster’s acknowledged AI-specific approach by requiring disclosure when AI functions as a co-author, without treating AI use or disclosure itself as grounds for an adverse inference.
qs: "Human in the loop": To ensure accuracy and trustworthiness, it is essential to check documents and material generated by AI.
In this regard, the party signing a document submitted to the Court bears responsibility for the accuracy and veracity of its contents.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The notice aligns with the cluster’s cautious, human-accountable framing by recognising both AI’s benefits and risks and withholding adjudicative use pending public consultation. It does not directly address substantive verification burdens or whether checking consumes efficiency gains, and its consultation commitment is weaker than an absolute bar on automated judgment.
qs: The Court recognizes both the risks and benefits of AI, and the potential for bias in AI programs, their underlying algorithms, and data sets.
For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Court’s notice aligns with selective, human-governed deployment: it recognizes both benefits and risks, including bias, while withholding automated judicial decision-making absent public consultation. It supports the cluster’s caution against treating AI as generally competent, though it does not provide task-level evidence or a broader work-redesign model.
qs: The Court recognizes both the risks and benefits of AI, and the potential for bias in AI programs, their underlying algorithms, and data sets.
For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.

kp.d: The amended notice requires counsel, parties and interveners to disclose directly AI-generated content in materials prepared for litigation and submitted to the Federal Court. A Declaration in the document's first paragraph must identify whether AI generated the entire document or specified paragraphs. The requirement is a notification measure, intended to inform the Court and other parties rather than establish an adverse inference.
qs: This shall be done by a Declaration in the first paragraph stating that AI was used in preparing the document, either in its entirety or only for specifically identified paragraphs (the “Declaration”).
For greater certainty, the Declaration is only intended to notify the Court and parties so that they can govern themselves accordingly.

kp.k: Disclosure distinguishes AI co-authorship from human-controlled editing
kp.d: Disclosure turns on AI directly supplying content, not whether it comes from an external web-based tool. AI suggestions, recommendations or critiques of human-written content do not require a Declaration where a human considers and manually implements changes. The notice also excludes non-generative systems that merely follow preset instructions.
qs: A Declaration is required when the role AI plays in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation resembles that of a co-author.

However, a Declaration is not required if AI was used to merely suggest changes, provide recommendations, or critique content already created by a human who could then consider and manually implement the changes.
This Notice does not apply to AI that lacks the creative ability to generate new content.

kp.k: Expert reports follow a separate disclosure route
kp.d: The notice excludes Certified Tribunal Records submitted by tribunals or other third-party decision-makers and expert reports. For expert reports, the Court states its understanding that AI use ought to be disclosed through the methodology summary under the Expert Witnesses Code of Conduct, as referred to in Rule 52.2 of the Federal Courts Rules.
qs: For greater certainty, this Notice does not apply to: (i) Certified Tribunal Records submitted by tribunals or other third-party decision-makers, or (ii) Expert reports, which the Court understands ought to require disclosure of the use of AI in the summary of methodology used under subparagraph 3(i) of the Expert Witnesses Code of Conduct as referred to in Rule 52.2 of the Federal Courts Rules.

kp.k: Successor counsel must investigate inherited materials
kp.d: Recognizing that new counsel may struggle to identify AI-generated content in previously filed documents or transferred drafts, the Court expects best efforts to ascertain its presence. Counsel should provide a Declaration for materials they have reason to believe may contain such content; the notice does not demand certainty about inherited work.
qs: In these cases, it is reasonable to expect new counsel to make best efforts to ascertain whether any such content has been included in those materials, and to provide a Declaration in respect of any materials they have reason to believe may include such content.

kp.k: Human verification remains essential to legal accuracy
kp.d: The Court urges verification of AI-created content and caution with AI-generated legal references and analysis. It identifies official court websites, established commercial publishers and trusted public services such as CanLII as reliable sources. These are professional safeguards recommended by the Court, not empirical findings about tool accuracy.
qs: "Human in the loop": To ensure accuracy and trustworthiness, it is essential to check documents and material generated by AI.
The Court urges verification of any AI-created content in these documents.
When referring to jurisprudence, statutes, policies, or commentaries in documents submitted to the Court, it is crucial to use only well-recognized and reliable sources.

kp.k: AI use leaves signatory responsibility and standards unchanged
kp.d: A Declaration alone will not attract an adverse inference, nor will AI use outside the notice's content-generation scope. Parties and interveners remain subject to existing Federal Courts Rules standards, and the person signing a submission remains responsible for its accuracy and veracity.
qs: The Court confirms that the inclusion of a Declaration, in and of itself, will not attract an adverse inference by the Court.
Parties and interveners will continue to be held to the existing standards under the Federal Courts Rules.
In this regard, the party signing a document submitted to the Court bears responsibility for the accuracy and veracity of its contents.

kp.k: Client unfamiliarity warrants considering human-only services
kp.d: The Court identifies ethical and access-to-justice issues where clients are unfamiliar with AI and its applications. Before using AI in proceedings, it encourages counsel to consider traditional human services if clients may not understand or wish to use AI. This is encouragement, not an express prohibition or mandatory consent requirement.
qs: Further, the Court understands that there are both ethical and access to justice issues regarding a lawyer’s use of AI when their client may not be familiar with AI and its various applications.

Before using AI in a proceeding, the Court encourages counsel to consider providing traditional, human services to clients if there is reason to believe a client may not be familiar with, or may not wish to use, AI.

kp.k: Uniform disclosure seeks fairness for self-represented litigants
kp.d: The Court explains that counsel's duties as Officers of the Court do not extend to self-represented individuals. Rather than let counsel rely solely on those duties while imposing elevated AI-specific responsibilities on self-represented parties, it adopts a notice intended to treat represented and self-represented parties and interveners fairly.
qs: It would be unfair to place elevated AI-related responsibilities only on these self-represented individuals, and allow counsel to rely on their duties.
Therefore, the Court provides this Notice to ensure fair treatment of all represented and self-represented parties and interveners.

kp.k: Potential benefits coexist with integrity and bias concerns
kp.d: The Court recognizes substantial potential benefits for document preparation while reporting concerns about hallucinations, deepfakes, fabricated legal authorities and governmental generative decision-making tools. It also recognizes potential bias in AI programs, algorithms and datasets. These concerns motivate safeguards for judicial integrity, public confidence and the rule of law; the notice provides no measured incidence or quantified benefits.
qs: The Court recognizes that AI may offer substantial benefits in the preparation of documents.

Significant concerns continue to be raised regarding the use of AI in Court proceedings, including with respect to “hallucinations”1 and “deepfakes”2, the potential fabrication of legal authorities through AI, and the use of generative decision-making tools by government officials.
The Court recognizes both the risks and benefits of AI, and the potential for bias in AI programs, their underlying algorithms, and data sets.

kp.k: Judicial AI decision-making requires prior public consultation
kp.d: The Court commits not to use AI, specifically automated decision-making tools, to make decisions or render judgments without first consulting the public. It also commits to periodic guidance updates as its understanding evolves and continuing stakeholder consultation through its Artificial Intelligence Working Group. This is a conditional institutional commitment, not an unconditional permanent ban.
qs: For its part, the Court will not use AI, and more specifically automated decision-making tools, to make its decisions or render its judgments, without first engaging in public consultation.
The Court will continue to update this guidance periodically as the Court’s understanding of AI evolves.
The Court is committed to full transparency and continuing consultations with respect to future iterations of this Notice through the Court’s Artificial Intelligence Working Group.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Federal Court of Canada recognizes potential document-preparation benefits and increasing reliance on AI, while identifying risks to litigation integrity and prescribing disclosure and human verification.
pts.d: In its amended notice, signed by Chief Justice Paul S. Crampton, the Court states that AI may substantially benefit document preparation and that litigation participants and administrative bodies may increasingly rely on or be affected by AI. It identifies concerns about fabricated facts and authorities, deepfakes, bias, and generative decision-making by government officials. Its concrete procedural response is to require disclosure when AI acts like a co-author of litigation materials and to urge verification of AI-created content. These are institutional requirements and guidance, rather than predictions of productivity gains or lawyer displacement. The Court maintains existing responsibility for document accuracy and says disclosure alone will not attract an adverse inference. It also identifies ethical and access-to-justice issues where clients are unfamiliar with AI, without claiming that AI expands access to legal help.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The notice relies on the Court's institutional authority, stakeholder consultation, and existing professional and procedural standards, not empirical performance evidence.
pts.d: The Court attributes the development of its approach to stakeholder consultations and feedback. It grounds disclosure in protecting judicial integrity, public confidence, and the rule of law, and grounds verification in existing professional standards. It references the Federal Courts Rules and the Expert Witnesses Code of Conduct for responsibility and expert-methodology disclosure. It supplies no quantified productivity findings, measured hallucination rates, benchmarks, or named incidents to substantiate the stated benefits and risks. Those statements are expressed as possibilities and concerns.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 7, 2024 notice sets present procedural expectations with narrowly defined triggers; increasing AI reliance has no specified forecast horizon.
pts.d: The declaration applies to materials both submitted to the Court and prepared for litigation when they contain content generated directly by AI, regardless of whether it came from an external application. It must appear in the first paragraph and identify whether AI generated the whole document or particular paragraphs. It does not apply merely because AI recommended or critiqued changes that a human manually implemented, or because non-generative automation was used. Certified Tribunal Records are excluded; expert reports are excluded from this declaration regime because the Court understands AI use should instead be disclosed in their methodology under the Expert Witnesses Code of Conduct. Successor counsel are expected to make best efforts to identify AI content in inherited materials. The Court promises periodic updates as understanding evolves, without a schedule, and conditions its own use of AI to make decisions or render judgments on prior public consultation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern Federal Court counsel, represented and self-represented parties, interveners, and their clients, rather than legal-market segments generally.
pts.d: Counsel, parties, and interveners must disclose qualifying AI-generated content and consider the stated principles. The Court explicitly seeks equal treatment of represented and self-represented participants rather than relying solely on lawyers' officer-of-the-court duties. Successor counsel face a best-efforts inquiry into inherited materials. Clients unfamiliar with AI or unwilling to use it are identified as a group for whom counsel should consider traditional human services. The Court and opposing parties receive notice so they can respond appropriately. The public's confidence in justice and administrative bodies whose decisions are challenged are also identified as affected interests. No firm-size, staffing, pricing, employment, or market-share effects are asserted.
